# Requisite variety: why an AI system needs as many responses as it has kinds of trouble

*An Ultrastable white paper. Ultrastable is the foundation for any autonomous system.*

## Executive summary

Many people believe that a capable enough model can handle any failure by trying again. This paper argues otherwise: a retry is one response. A system facing many kinds of failure needs many kinds of response, and needs a way to grow new ones. That is Ashby's law, and it can be read from the system's own records.

Ashby's law of requisite variety says a regulator can only hold its outcomes steady if it can answer each kind of disturbance with a fitting response. An AI system that meets every failure with the same retry has one response. We state the law as checks on this system's own records: does every loop have a way to close, does every failure get its own repair item, and does the second loop actually add new responses.

It is written for people who build or run AI systems and want them to keep working without someone watching. It names 3 concrete problems, the mechanism that answers each one, and how to put that mechanism in place.

## 1. The problem

Only variety in the regulator can absorb variety in the disturbances. If the environment can throw more kinds of trouble at a system than the system has distinct responses, some outcomes will leave their limits no matter how well each response is tuned. [1]

This matters now because the usual answer, retrying is enough, sends teams after the wrong fix. A better model or another reviewer does not close a loop that nothing checks.

The problems in detail:

1. A loop with no response at all. A loop that has no closing probe and no server-side owner contributes no variety: nothing in it answers a disturbance. Every registered loop should carry both. [1]
2. A regulator that never adds a response. When the first loop's responses are not enough, the system has to gain new ones. Here that is the second loop changing a parameter. If it never steps, the system's variety is fixed at whatever it was built with. [1]
3. A response that is never checked against the world. Variety only counts if the response actually lands. A deploy that is not read back live may be a response that did nothing. [1]

## 2. The approach

The approach follows Ashby's ultrastable system [2]: a first loop acts on the world, and a second loop changes the first loop's settings whenever a variable that matters leaves its limits, and keeps changing them until it is back inside.

Ultrastable is that design as working code [3]. For each problem above it uses a specific mechanism:

1. A loop with no response at all: every loop declares a closing probe and a server owner (SERVER-OWNS-LOOPS-1, `instances/ultrastable/loop-registry.json`)
2. A regulator that never adds a response: reads unregulated disturbance classes from the work queue (ASHBY-KERNEL-1, `seed/worker/src/regulation.js`); steps a parameter when a variable stays out of limits (ULTRASTABILITY-1, `foundation/ultrastability.py`)
3. A response that is never checked against the world: every item names a live closing probe (SPEC-GATE-1, `seed/scripts/specgate.py`)

## 3. Putting it into practice

To apply this to your own system, one step per problem:

1. A loop with no response at all. Put in place: every loop declares a closing probe and a server owner. Check it with one number, share of registered loops that declare a closing probe and a server-side owner, and set a limit for it (>= 1.0 is the limit we use).
2. A regulator that never adds a response. Put in place: reads unregulated disturbance classes from the work queue. Check it with one number, second-order steps the ultrastability loop took in the last 30 days (ops/ultrastability.jsonl), and set a limit for it (>= 1 is the limit we use).
3. A response that is never checked against the world. Put in place: every item names a live closing probe. Check it with one number, share of uploaded deploys proven live against their commit, and set a limit for it (>= 0.95 is the limit we use).

In our own system, 3 of 3 of these checks pass today. Share of registered loops that declare a closing probe and a server-side owner reads 1.0 (n = 120; source: instances/ultrastable/loop-registry.json (declared)). Second-order steps the ultrastability loop took in the last 30 days (ops/ultrastability.jsonl) reads 172 (n = 23089; source: ops/ultrastability.jsonl). Share of uploaded deploys proven live against their commit reads 0.999 (n = 720; source: ops/deploys.jsonl (same window)). Where a check fails, a work item carries the fix, and it closes only when the same check passes.

## 4. Trade-offs and limits

- We state the law in our own words from chapter 11. We do not count disturbance classes directly; we read proxies from the loop registry, the second loop's log and the deploy ledger.
- A declared closing probe is a response on paper. The deploy check is the only reading here that shows a response worked live.
- Scale. One organization: 500 closed pull requests (360 merged) over 7.85 days. Our numbers describe this system; they are not a causal estimate and are not compared with the study's effect sizes as if they were.
- Who wrote the changes. 87% of merged pull requests in the window were opened by code agent sessions run under the owner's account, not by the system's own loops. The latest criticality tick puts the system in the driven regime with 0 self-originated deploys, so most of the work measured here was started from outside.
- Review by construction. Ultrastable has no human review step, so a short open-to-merge time is partly a consequence of the design. The real test of the design is quality: the revert and deploy-verification findings, which can fail.
- Revert share counts commits whose subject starts with Revert; a fix that undoes a change without that word is not counted, so the figure is a lower bound.
- Source. Book, version 1956; its findings may change in later versions.
